title: Operator eye view: inference economics, operator risk, and go-to-market talking points
content:
Purpose and audience:
This note is a concise field guide for SDRs, SEs, and product marketing to have operator-centric, economics-first conversations with infra/platform/ML engineering buyers who are evaluating self-hosted stacks (vLLM / Text Generation Inference / TensorRT-LLM families) vs. Redwood managed offerings.

TL;DR:
- Self-hosted stacks can be attractive on headline compute cost but hide persistent operational costs: scaling, model compatibility, quantization tuning, memory/kv cache engineering, and incident remediation. Redwood’s win threads: predictable unit economics, integrated fallbacks, deployment abstraction across hosted/dedicated/private, and operator time savings (weeks/months not hours).

Buyer signals (strong indicators they are evaluating build):
- “We want to run everything in our VPC / air-gapped environment.”
- “We need full control of model weights and quantization knobs.”
- “We already have GPU capacity and want to reduce cloud bills.”
- “We have an internal infra team that owns inference endpoints.”

Why operators pick self-hosted (what they believe):
- Apparent lower $/token if you amortize GPUs across many workloads.
- Keeps data fully controlled on-prem or in a VPC.
- Full control of model deployment cadence and binary/runtime versions.

Reality checks / hidden costs operators often underweight:
1) Engineering time: tuning batching policies, KV cache sharding, and memory layouts for different models is iterative and model-specific. Expect 1–3 FTE-months to reach stable runbook for a single LLM family.
2) Operational volatility: model upgrades can shift memory and latency characteristics and break autoscaling rules.
3) Reliability & runbooks: On-call load for degraded KV cache or attention kernel faults requires deep inference runtime expertise.
4) Quality regressions: Quantization and kernel choices affect output quality—regression detection and rollback tooling costs more than common expectation.
5) Cost leakage: Idle reserved GPUs, inefficient packing, and cold-start overheads inflate realized $/token vs simulated numbers.

Practical comparison (operator-focused):
- vLLM ecosystem (open-source continuous-batching runtime)
  - Strengths: fast prototyping, tight integration with custom tokenizers and schedulers, community kernels for newer model families.
  - Weaknesses: shard/packing complexity, limited enterprise-grade monitoring, manual fallback strategies.
  - Typical operator ask: “Can we host it on our fleet and tune batch windows?”

- TGI (NVIDIA Text Generation Inference / Hugging Face TGI-like stacks)
  - Strengths: good performance on NVIDIA stacks with prebuilt containers, integration with HF models, growing community tooling.
  - Weaknesses: version compatibility, ops burden for multi-tenant isolation, and tuning required for KV-heavy chat workloads.
  - Typical operator ask: “How do we handle model drift and runtime upgrades safely?”

- TensorRT-LLM family (optimized kernels / quantized execution)
  - Strengths: maximum throughput for supported models, excellent latency when fully tuned on target hardware.
  - Weaknesses: brittle model support surface, complex build chains, hardware lock-in and expensive debugging.
  - Typical operator ask: “Can we get 3–4x throughput gains for specific ffowards?”

Where Redwood wins (customer pain we solve):
- Predictable unit economics: token-level billing and transparent cost-of-serving dashboards so customers can compare apples-to-apples against their self-hosted run-rates.
- Unified API + rollout primitives: same semantics across hosted, dedicated, private; easy canary/rollback without changing code.
- Automated fallbacks & routing: policy-driven fallbacks to cheaper model variants or alternate regions when capacity is constrained.
- Observability built for inference: per-token latency distribution, cold-start heatmaps, KV cache hit rates, and quality regression hooks tied to test prompts.
- Ops load reduction: we surface recommended batching/cache/quantization profiles per workload so teams avoid repeated engineering cycles.

Quantitative econ sketch (text table for field use):
- Inputs to share with buyers: current RPS, average prompt length (tokens in), average completion length (tokens out), peak concurrency, target p99 latency SLO, existing GPU inventory and utilization.
- Quick comparator outputs (talking numbers, not promises):
  - Self-hosted headline: GPU hours * price + ops FTE cost amortized (assume 0.5–2.0 FTE depending on complexity) + SRE on-call premiums.
  - Redwood hosted: per-token + model surcharge (predictable).
  - Key seller point: 20–40% of self-hosted TCO often sits in ops and leakage (packing inefficiency, cold starts).

Operator risk checklist (rapid probe during discovery):
- Do you have dedicated infra owners for inference tuning?
- Have you run controlled A/B tests for quantized vs fp16 weights across your eval prompts?
- Can your current monitoring detect output quality regression (not just latency/errors)?
- Do you accept model version drift without a fast rollback plan?
- Are your teams comfortable triaging kernel-level CUDA/TRT failures?

Common objections and short rebuttals for sellers:
- Objection: “We already own GPUs — managed will never beat our raw $/token.”
  - Rebuttal: "Raw cost excludes ops, packing inefficiencies, and time-to-stable. Let’s model your peak and idle utilization and compare realized $/effective-token rather than sticker GPU price."
- Objection: “We need air-gapped data handling.”
  - Rebuttal: "Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem deployments with KMS/HSM integration and audit logs — you keep control while we handle runtime ops patterns."
- Objection: “We need fine-grained control over quantization and kernels.”
  - Rebuttal: "We expose quantization profiles and model variant controls, and we’ll work with your infra team to validate profiles on your eval suite before rollout."

Sales hooks and recommended snippets (two-line soundbites):
- "Keep the model you want; outsource the hardest part — making inference predictable and inexpensive in production."
- "We’ll show you realized $/token including packing and ops overheads — most teams find managed becomes cheaper at scale once ops time is included."

Migration lanes (practical lanes we recommend):
1) Proof-of-concept: start with hosted API on non-sensitive workloads; compare latency/cost with your self-hosted POC over 2–4 weeks.
2) Dedicated pilot: run a single critical workload on Dedicated (reserved capacity) to measure tail latency and costs with near-production traffic.
3) Private trial & validation: if required for compliance, move to Private with a limited fleet and joint runbook development.

Onboarding friction map (what will slow deals and how to remove blockers):
- Keys: data residency, model binary trust, SLA/legal terms, access to internal eval prompts.
- Remove friction by: providing a short NDA + private onboarding plan, a joint quantization validation checklist, and a prebuilt Prometheus/OpenTelemetry integration for their SRE team.

Competitive artifacts to leave behind (for SEs):
- One-pager: "Realized cost comparison worksheet" (spreadsheet with inputs for GPU type, utilization, ops FTE amortization).
- Runbook template: "Rollback & fallback playbook for model upgrade incidents."
- Eval harness snapshot: minimal set of prompts to detect hallucination and latency regressions post-quantization.

Open questions for product/eng to support sales motion:
- Can we publish a short guide mapping common open-source stacks -> expected toil and a recommended Redwood config for parity?
- Can eng provide three ready-made quantization+batch profiles (chat, classification, embeddings) as starting points?
- Should we produce a small benchmark harness that customers can run on their fleet to show packing inefficiencies?

Next steps for GTM team (owners indicated):
- Create spreadsheet template for "realized $/token" (owner: Miguel Ortiz).
- Build SE playbook slides with the operator risk checklist and one-pager artifacts (owner: Lena Huang).
- Draft a short customer testimonial script from an early Dedicated customer that highlights ops time savings (owner: Tom Becker).

Appendix — short technical notes for SEs:
- KV cache behavior: self-hosted systems often require manual cache sharding/pinning; Redwood’s runtime manages eviction and hot-hot shards automatically, reducing long-tail latency incidents.
- Quantization regressions: mitigation pattern = shadow quantized traffic + output-diff metrics + prompt-based quality gates before switch. Offer to run this for customer as part of onboarding.
- Model routing: policy-based routing (latency vs cost) is a low-effort win to reduce spend without engineering separate endpoints.

This document is intentionally concise — use it as a crib sheet in discovery and handoffs. Keep a copy of the spreadsheet and the runbook template in the SE kit and iterate the messaging as we gather real deal anecdotes.
